steps.text: Identify the indication for giving medication via a nebuliser (e.g. can't use an inhaler because of confusion or hand problems; lots of mucus; really struggling to breathe).
Perform hand hygiene.
Complete a respiratory history and examination first. If the medication is urgent, at least auscultate the chest for adventitious sounds (wheezes, crackles) so you can compare before and after.
Check the medication chart for a valid order written by a doctor and follow the six rights of safe administration.
Gather equipment: nebuliser compressor, medication chamber, mask or mouthpiece, tubing, liquid medication, drug order (medication chart).
Perform hand hygiene.
Introduce yourself (full name and designation). Verify identity (full name and date of birth) and check allergies.
Explain what you are going to do and obtain consent.
Position the person semi-Fowler's or sitting upright.
Plug the nebuliser machine into a power outlet and turn it on at the wall.
Check right medication, dose, route and time against the drug order.
Connect the tubing to the nebuliser chamber (before adding the medication, to avoid spillage).
Add the liquid medication to one side of the chamber, screw the two sides together and attach the mask or mouthpiece.
Place the mask over the face, or give the mouthpiece and ask the person to seal their lips around it and breathe normally.
Turn the nebuliser on and start nebulising (a standard dose takes about 5-10 minutes). If oxygen is used instead of the compressor, always monitor SpO2.
Document/sign that you have given the medication (the sixth right: documentation).
When fully nebulised, turn the compressor off and remove the mask/mouthpiece.
Reassess breathing and respiratory rate, and auscultate the lung fields to evaluate effectiveness.
Clean equipment: rinse the chamber; mask/mouthpiece and tubing can stay with the person for next time.
Perform hand hygiene.
Document the treatment in the progress notes/chart, including breath sounds before and after.
Evaluate the treatment plan and reassess at regular intervals or as required.
Communicate any changes in the person's condition to the treating doctor.
Check the medication order, patient identity, allergies, expiry date and indication against the medication chart; do the 5 rights 3 times.
Explain the procedure and obtain consent.
Prepare the nebuliser equipment and medication safely.
Position the patient upright.
Apply the prescribed air flow according to local instructions.
Encourage normal tidal breathing through the mouthpiece/mask.
Monitor respiratory status and response with a respiratory assessment.
Stop and escalate if deterioration occurs.
Clean, dispose of or reuse equipment according to policy.
Document medication, route/device, response and any adverse effects.

notes.text: A nebuliser pushes compressed air through liquid medication, turning it into a mist the person inhales through a simple face mask or mouthpiece. A puffer with a spacer works just as effectively for most people and is more convenient.
93225 Lecture 2: set the nebuliser to 6-8 L/min. If it is set too high (above 10 L/min) the medication is delivered too fast, reducing effectiveness, and it may pop the connection off the air port.

Relievers (e.g. salbutamol/Ventolin) are fast-acting bronchodilators that relax airway muscle. Preventers (e.g. fluticasone/Flixotide, budesonide/Pulmicort) are corticosteroids that reduce airway swelling, redness and mucus.
Clinical safety alert: clean and maintain nebulisers after each use, or the person risks infection and/or not getting the right dose. At home, replace mask, mouthpiece and tubing every three months.
Children: a mask lets the child breathe naturally. Demonstrate on a doll or toy, let them play with the equipment, and sitting on a parent's lap can help.

Driving gas differs between sources (see CONFLICTS). TSANZ: in COPD and chronic respiratory failure, give bronchodilators by MDI and spacer, or if a nebuliser is necessary it should be air-driven with oxygen continued via nasal cannulae. The Lab 2 workbook says 'prescribed air flow'. Section 12.6 says hospitals often use oxygen instead of the compressor, with SpO2 monitored.
